results.title: FAQ — Woomool
results.content:
That graph tells you which notes are related, but not what they say. To follow your own thinking, you still have to open each note and read it.

Woomool is built around the graph itself. It breaks your thinking into small, separate ideas, and each one sits on the canvas as a node you can read. When you look at a Woomool graph, you see the thoughts themselves and how they fit together. The graph is the thinking, not a map of where it’s stored.

Woomool also has a voice AI agent built in. Think out loud, and the agent adds and connects ideas on the canvas as you speak. Obsidian doesn’t offer anything like that out of the box.

## How is Woomool different from Notion?

Notion is great for organizing work that has already taken shape: docs, wikis, databases, and project plans. [...] Woomool helps during the meeting. As people talk, the discussion appears as a live graph on one canvas that every participant sees. Watching the conversation take shape changes it: the group notices which ideas connect, which questions are still open, and what’s missing, while there’s still time to do something about it.

Woomool’s AI also works for you in the moment. Say “Hey Ziggy” and ask it to add an idea, connect two threads, or restructure part of the graph, all by voice and without breaking the flow of the meeting. [...] ## What is Woomool?

Woomool is an extended mind for visionaries: people who carry a lot of ideas and plans for a long time, and need to share them with the people they build with.

You talk or type, and Woomool’s AI agent turns your thinking into a graph on a shared canvas. Each idea becomes its own small node, connected to the ideas around it. You can take in the shape of your whole thinking at a glance, and the graph is still there the next time you pick it up.

## How is Woomool different from Obsidian?

Obsidian is built around documents. You write notes and link them together, and the graph view draws each note as a dot and each link as a line.

results.title: AI Is Fueling A Flood Of Customer Complaints. Is That A Bad Thing?
results.content:
So how should businesses respond to this flood of AI-generated complaints? And how can consumers make sure their genuine grievances don't get lost in a sea of AI slop?

## Why Is There A Flood Of AI Complaints, And What's The Problem?

It's easy to see why people turn to AI when they have a complaint.

Many of us struggle with the dreaded blank page. We know something has gone wrong, but putting our frustration into words, explaining what happened and making a convincing case can be surprisingly difficult.

With a simple prompt and a few personal details, ChatGPT or Claude can produce a polished complaint letter in seconds, clearly outlining the problem and explaining why we're unhappy. [...] And that neatly captures the dilemma. AI is making complaints more accessible, but it's also making them harder to process.

## Should You Use AI To Write Complaints?

Absolutely. In principle, there's nothing wrong with using AI to help write a complaint.

Getting our thoughts down clearly can be difficult, particularly when we're angry, frustrated or unsure about our rights. AI can help organize our arguments, explain what went wrong and communicate what we want the company to do about it.

There's even some evidence that AI-assisted complaints can lead to better outcomes.

But there are a few important things to remember. [...] And importantly, this means people who might previously have given up can now make their voices heard.

Think about it. In the past, how many people simply accepted poor service, unfair treatment or a disappointing product because complaining seemed like more trouble than it was worth? AI removes much of that friction, potentially bringing legitimate problems to light that businesses might otherwise never hear about.

But there's a catch.

AI doesn't always know when to stop talking.

A review of the impact of AI-generated complaints across 11 countries found that submissions had increased in length in 76 of the 84 cases studied.

Many contained unnecessary details, irrelevant arguments and, in some cases, abusive or threatening language.

results.title: AI Customer Service Frustration: Why People Prefer People | AnswerConnect
results.content:
1 in 3 said that talking to an AI agent or chatbot is the single most frustrating experience when contacting a business. And when we delved deeper, the data showed a clear pattern:

- 51% say AI struggles to understand their needs
- 48% say AI cannot resolve their problem
- 35% say AI gives inaccurate information
- 31% say AI lacks empathy

AI is supposed to make customer service more convenient. But for many callers, it’s doing the opposite. Instead of getting answers, they’re getting stuck in frustrating loops that waste time, cause confusion, and break trust.

## When AI fails, customers notice [...] ## Key takeaways

- AI frustration is rising. 1 in 3 customers say interacting with AI is the most frustrating part of contacting a business, and that they will simply hang up if connected to AI.
- AI often fails to understand or resolve issues, leading to repeated explanations and inaccurate responses.
- Customers still prefer people. 83% say they would rather speak to a real person than an AI agent.
- Poor AI experiences are brand-damaging – they decrease trustand can push customers toward competitors.
- Human receptionists create better experiences, resolving problems faster while building loyalty.

Source for stats: OnePoll [...] Watch the real call below to hear the full exchange.

Beyond the technical errors, what stands out most is the growing frustration. The AI struggles to understand context, fails to answer simple questions, and ultimately cannot move the conversation forward. This is why when people call a business and are connected to AI, 29% hang up immediately. That’s almost one in three people lost before the conversation even begins.

This isn’t just a technology problem. It’s a customer experience problem.

results.title: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints - AOL
results.content:
You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complaints process is accessible to tenants, but AI-generated complaints don’t help with this. Sending a complaint can be intimidating and time-consuming, and using AI can give someone confidence, but when we speak to customers in person or over the phone, and reference the same technical language that’s in their AI-generated complaint letter, they often don’t understand what we are saying. [...] It is much better to receive a human-written complaint (even with spelling mistakes and expletives), because at least it comes from the person, and gets to the heart of the issue. It means we can help you to the best of our ability, because you have told us exactly what you need. Additionally, AI enables our regular complainants.

“Frequent flyers” are part of any complaints role, but receiving multiple, massive, AI-generated complaints a month from someone makes us feel as if they don’t see us as people worthy of respect. Our organisation is considering classing this as a form of harassment, and it can’t come soon enough. Name and address supplied [...] # How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints

The Guardian

Re your article (‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints.
